{"id": "fc0151d7-64e1-4455-89ae-985464b5b192", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Cold starts are the classic culprit here — when a Lambda function hasn't been invoked for a while, AWS reclaims its execution environment. The next request has to spin up a fresh one: downloading your code/layers, starting the runtime, and running any initialization code (imports, DB connections, SDK clients, etc.) before your handler even runs. That init overhead only shows up on that first "cold" invocation; subsequent requests reuse the warm environment and skip it.

Common factors that make cold starts worse:
- **Larger deployment packages / more layers** — more to download and unpack
- **VPC-attached functions** — ENI setup used to add real overhead (much less so today, but still a factor)
- **Runtime choice** — Java/.NET typically cold-start slower than Python/Node/Go
- **Heavy init code** — SDK client setup, config loading, DB connections done outside the handler
- **Low memory allocation** — memory size also scales CPU, so smaller functions init slower
- **No provisioned concurrency** — nothing keeping environments warm during idle periods
